subskill: Integer optimum: counting tied whole-number plans
prompt: A pottery studio makes bowls and vases. Each bowl needs 20 minutes of wheel time and 20 ounces of clay, and each vase needs 30 minutes of wheel time and 12 ounces of clay. This week the studio has 580 minutes of wheel time and 404 ounces of clay. The studio earns a profit of $36 on each bowl and $24 on each vase, and only whole bowls and vases are made. How many different weekly plans (numbers of bowls and vases) earn the largest profit the studio can make?
explanation: Let x be the number of bowls and y the number of vases. The constraints are 20x + 30y ≤ 580 (that is, 2x + 3y ≤ 58) and 20x + 12y ≤ 404 (that is, 5x + 3y ≤ 101), with x and y whole numbers, and the profit is 36x + 24y = 12(3x + 2y). The two boundary lines meet at x = 43/3 ≈ 14.33, y = 88/9 ≈ 9.78, which is not a whole-number plan. Rounding both down gives (14, 9) with 3x + 2y = 60, but that is not the best whole-number plan: (14, 10) is allowed (2(14) + 3(10) = 58 and 5(14) + 3(10) = 100) and gives 3x + 2y = 62. A value of 63 would need 3x + 2y = 63 inside the region; the real maximum of 3x + 2y is about 62.6, so 62 is the best possible, a profit of $744. Plans with 3x + 2y = 62 differ by steps of (+2, -3): (12, 13) breaks the wheel limit (24 + 39 = 63 > 58), (14, 10) and (16, 7) work (5(16) + 3(7) = 101), and (18, 4) breaks the clay limit (90 + 12 = 102 > 101). So exactly 2 plans earn the largest profit. Choice 4 counts the plans earning $720, the profit of the rounded-down corner (14, 9), which is not the largest profit. Choice 11 counts every whole-number solution of 3x + 2y = 62 (x = 0, 2, 4, ..., 20) without checking either limit. Choice 5 swaps the two profits ($24 per bowl and $36 per vase).
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>20*x+30*y<=580&&20*x+12*y<=404;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=36*x+24*y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n

distractor_solve.5: const ok=(x,y)=>20*x+30*y<=580&&20*x+12*y<=404;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=24*x+36*y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n
distractor_solve.11: const ok=(x,y)=>20*x+30*y<=580&&20*x+12*y<=404;let best=-1;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y))best=Math.max(best,36*x+24*y);let n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(36*x+24*y===best)n++;return n

subskill: Integer optimum: tied plans for the most items
prompt:
A shipping crate can hold a total mass of at most 133 kilograms and a total volume of at most 179 liters. It will be packed with boxes of two types, P and Q, described in the table below.
Box type | Mass (kilograms) | Volume (liters)
P | 9 | 13
Q | 10 | 11
Only whole boxes are packed. The crate is to hold as many boxes as possible in total. How many different combinations of type P and type Q boxes achieve this?
explanation: Let p and q be the numbers of type P and type Q boxes. The crate requires 9p + 10q ≤ 133 and 13p + 11q ≤ 179, and the goal is to make p + q as large as possible. The two boundary lines meet at p ≈ 10.55, q ≈ 3.81, where p + q ≈ 14.35, so no plan can hold 15 boxes. Rounding the corner down gives (10, 3), only 13 boxes, so the best whole-number plans have to be found directly: test p + q = 14. Mass requires 9p + 10(14 - p) ≤ 133, so 140 - p ≤ 133 and p ≥ 7. Volume requires 13p + 11(14 - p) ≤ 179, so 2p + 154 ≤ 179 and p ≤ 12.5, so p ≤ 12. Thus p = 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12, giving (7, 7), (8, 6), (9, 5), (10, 4), (11, 3) and (12, 2): 6 combinations. Choice 1 treats the rounded corner as the single best plan without checking which other combinations reach the greatest total. Choice 8 swaps the masses of the two box types (10 kilograms for P and 9 for Q), which changes the mass bound and the count. Choice 13 counts the 14-box combinations that satisfy the volume limit (p ≤ 12) but never checks the mass limit.
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>9*x+10*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=x+y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n

distractor_solve.8: const ok=(x,y)=>10*x+9*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=x+y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n
distractor_solve.13: const ok=(x,y)=>9*x+10*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y))best=Math.max(best,x+y);let n=0;for(let x=0;x<=best;x++){const y=best-x;if(13*x+11*y<=179)n++}return n

subskill: Integer optimum: item total in the best whole-number order
prompt: A garden shop is ordering planters and bird feeders to sell at a fair. Each planter costs the shop $11 and earns a profit of $26, and each bird feeder costs the shop $6 and earns a profit of $14. The shop can spend at most $133 on the order, and it must order at least 7 bird feeders. Only whole items are ordered, and every item ordered will be sold. In the order that gives the greatest total profit, what is the total number of planters and bird feeders?
explanation: Let x be the number of planters and y the number of bird feeders: 11x + 6y ≤ 133, y ≥ 7, and the profit is 26x + 14y. Per dollar, a planter earns 26/11 ≈ 2.36 and a feeder 14/6 ≈ 2.33, so without the whole-number condition the shop would buy only the required 7 feeders and spend the rest on planters: x = (133 - 42)/11 ≈ 8.27. Rounding down gives (8, 7), which spends $130 and earns $306. But that is not the best whole-number order, because $3 is left unspent. Trading planters for feeders lets the order use the budget exactly: 11x + 6y = 133 has the whole-number solution (5, 13), which earns 26(5) + 14(13) = $312. Checking the other orders near the budget line, (6, 11) earns $310, (7, 9) earns $308, (8, 7) earns $306, and (4, 14), (3, 16), (2, 18), (1, 20), (0, 22) earn $300, $302, $304, $306, $308, so (5, 13) is the only best order, with 5 + 13 = 18 items. Choice 15 is the rounded corner (8, 7). Choice 13 comes from reading 'at least 7 bird feeders' as 'at most 7' (or dropping it): the best order is then (11, 2). Choice 16 swaps the two costs ($6 per planter, $11 per feeder).
solve: let best=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(11*x+6*y<=133&&y>=7){const v=26*x+14*y;if(v>best){best=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return bx+by

subskill: Integer optimum: coordinate difference of the best plan
prompt:
A workshop builds x chairs and y tables each week, where x and y are whole numbers. Its labor hours and machine hours limit the weekly plan to
5x + 7y ≤ 68
7x + 6y ≤ 84
and its weekly profit, in hundreds of dollars, is P = 5x + 6y. For the plan with the greatest weekly profit, how many more chairs than tables are built?
explanation: The boundary lines 5x + 7y = 68 and 7x + 6y = 84 meet at x = 180/19 ≈ 9.47, y = 56/19 ≈ 2.95, where P ≈ 65.05, so no whole-number plan earns more than 65. Rounding that corner to the nearest whole numbers gives (9, 3), which is allowed (45 + 21 = 66 ≤ 68 and 63 + 18 = 81 ≤ 84) but earns only P = 63; rounding both down gives (9, 2), which earns 57. P = 65 needs 5x + 6y = 65, whose whole-number solutions are (13, 0), (7, 5) and (1, 10): (13, 0) breaks the machine limit (91 > 84), and (7, 5) and (1, 10) break the labor limit (35 + 35 = 70 and 5 + 70 = 75 are more than 68). P = 64 needs 5x + 6y = 64, whose whole-number solutions are (8, 4) and (2, 9); (2, 9) breaks the labor limit (10 + 63 = 73 > 68), and (8, 4) satisfies both (40 + 28 = 68 and 56 + 24 = 80). So the best plan is 8 chairs and 4 tables, and 8 - 4 = 4. Choice 6 rounds the corner to the nearest whole numbers, (9, 3). Choice 7 rounds both corner coordinates down, (9, 2). Choice 12 swaps the two profit rates (P = 6x + 5y), whose best plan is (12, 0).
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>5*x+7*y<=68&&7*x+6*y<=84;let b=-1,bx=0,by=0,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=30;x++)for(let y=0;y<=30;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=5*x+6*y;if(v>b){b=v;bx=x;by=y;n=1}else if(v===b)n++}if(n!==1)throw new Error('tie');return bx-by

prompt: A crafts vendor makes wooden boxes and picture frames to sell each week. Each box uses $8 of materials and each frame uses $3 of materials, and the weekly materials budget is $91. explanation: Let x be the number of boxes and y the number of frames: 8x + 3y ≤ 91, x + y ≤ 21, and the profit is 10x + 4y. Rounding the corner down to 5 boxes leaves room for 16 frames, (5, 16), but that earns only $114. The profit 10x + 4y is always even, so $117 is impossible; try $116, that is, 5x + 2y = 58. Its whole-number solutions are (0, 29), (2, 24), (4, 19), (6, 14), (8, 9) and (10, 4). (0, 29), (2, 24) and (4, 19) have more than 21 items, and (10, 4) costs 80 + 12 = 92, more than $91, while (6, 14) costs 48 + 42 = 90 with 20 items and (8, 9) costs 64 + 27 = 91 with 17 items. So the plans earning the greatest profit, $116, are (6, 14) and (8, 9), and the greatest number of frames among them is 14. Choice 16 is the rounded corner (5, 16). Choice 9 gives the frames in the other best plan, (8, 9). Choice 8 gives the number of boxes in that plan instead of frames.
